title: Part 1
text: Ch 1 – Shifting Sands David blinked, clawing his way back up from the relative peace he had been drifting in, Or... he thought he did. It was hard to tell. Everything was dark, dry, and close, the grit scratching faintly against his eyelashes the only real proof his eyes were open at all. He tried to swallow. Instant regret. His throat seized on the attempt, dragged across a thick film of silt and dust that coated his mouth like wet plaster. The cough that followed didn’t come from his chest — it wrung him from the inside out, deep and rolling and loud in the otherwise perfect silence. Pain bloomed through his right shoulder like someone’d lit a flare inside the joint. Not enough to knock him out again — even if for a moment, his body strongly considered it — but enough to burn through the fog at the edge of his thoughts. That arm... where even was it? He shifted, or tried to. The shoulder was wrenched backward at an unnatural angle, trapped somewhere behind him. He couldn’t quite feel it. Not properly. Given the position, it was probably underneath him, and had been for quite some time. How long had he even been out? The air tasted stale. Not rot-stale, just... old . Like it had already been breathed once and politely declined a second use. It clung to the grit in his throat, and for a moment, he couldn’t tell if that was the room’s fault or his own. He tried to roll just enough to shift the pressure off the dead arm. No luck. Something sharp greeted him in every direction — jagged ribs of rubble mixed with the broader flat crush of stone slabs. They pressed in at odd angles, some stabbing through cloth to find skin, others just... there , forcing joints into unnatural postures and denying leverage entirely. The ground beneath him was cool and unmoving, a layer of compacted sand that offered no give and even less comfort. His left arm, at least, was mostly free. Curled near his head, though the space was tight enough he had to move slow just to avoid flaying himself against unseen edges. Fingers crept outward, brushing along the nearby debris. Rough, gritty surfaces met his touch — stone fractured under pressure, shedding streams of dry sand that whispered down onto his face in response. He stilled. Sand? ...Oh. Right. The walkway. The Eyrie. He remembered the brittle stretch of stone underfoot — just wide enough to make him run stupid, just thin enough to make him regret it. Nemesis had swung at him; he remembered that much. A wide, angry arc meant for bone, not structure. It hit a support pillar instead. The whole thing had come down like it was made of plaster and drywall, not ancient stone. He didn’t remember the fall itself — just the sound. The crack of crumbling masonry. A sharp impact. Then darkness. In hindsight, it must’ve taken more than just the walkway. Probably part of the stairwell too. There was way too much debris around him for this to be a single platform collapse. This was an avalanche . Bad maintenance and worse luck, stacked like bricks and now buried in his ribs. Funny thing was... the landing hadn’t even hurt. Not really. He’d hit the ground so hard, there hadn’t been time for pain. Just an impact. Then lights out. Waking up though? That was a different story. His head throbbed, low and deep and constant. Not sharp — just heavy, like the ache had weight. It pressed against the background noise of every other random pain that was gradually waking up and won the argument. Miraculously, his skull had held. No blood in his eyes. No dripping sounds. No open gash. Just a single jagged stone pressed against his temple, insistent and quiet. Not hard enough to break skin. But close. If he’d fallen just slightly to the left... His skull wouldn’t have stopped the blow. It would’ve caved. Like an egg. Hell of a mess, that would've made. Bits of him everywhere. Real inconvenience. He shut that thought down before it went anywhere useful. He swallowed down another cough, forcing it into silence with sheer will. The dust still clawed at the back of his throat, but he wasn’t about to trigger another body-wide shudder. Not with the rubble that had started treating him like a stress ball. Alright. Inventory time. Nothing felt missing . That was a start. His legs were there. Chest still intact, more or less. Bruised? Absolutely. Bleeding? Probably. Slightly crushed in places? Almost definitely. But still whole. The right arm though... He tried to flex the fingers. Nothing. No twitch. No sting. No pull in the tendons. There was just... absence . A hollow space where the arm should’ve existed in his mind. It wasn’t pain that unsettled him — it was the lack of it. That meant the limb had been pinned long enough to kill sensation. Great. That was gonna be a fun reintroduction once the nerves decided to clock back in. He couldn’t even tell if it was broken or just numb. Either way... Problem for later. He shifted his left arm carefully, slow enough to avoid brushing any sharp edges. The motion dragged across stone — rough, uneven — and he curled it inward, trying to map his own torso through the press of rubble. Chest. Side. Hip. Rubble. More rubble. A jagged piece jutting near his ribs. Everything was compact. Tight. Smothered. But not entirely immobile. Each movement sent a faint shiver through the pile. He could feel it above him — stones shifting, not much, but not nothing . Grains of sand trickled down the back of his neck. A whisper of weight. Somewhere near his shoulder, a chunk of debris let out a gritty sigh and resettled. Just a little. The silence around him made it unbearable. It wasn’t dramatic. Nothing tumbled. Nothing cracked. But the rubble remembered it could move. And every breath he took was a nudge toward that decision. His elbow shifted back, catching the edge of a stone lightly. Something above him moved . The weight across his torso dipped, then ground slightly sideways, a low, gravelly slide that pressed new pain into his legs and kicked up another burst of dust. He froze. A larger block near his head scraped down half an inch with a lazy, predatory shrug. Instinct took over before thought could catch up — his left arm snapped upward, wedging between the stone and his face. Not to shove it back — he didn’t have that kind of leverage — but just to catch it. Slow it. Redirect it. If it came down further, it was going to hit something. Better the arm than the eye. The last dust stirred loose by the shift hit his lungs like sandpaper. He choked, sharp and sudden, and the cough tore through his body before he could stop it. Stone dug deeper into his side as his ribs convulsed, and a fresh spray of pebbles tumbled down his collarbone — dry, biting, unkind. Above him, the ceiling of stone responded. It shifted again. Just once. Then — mercifully — it stopped. His chest heaved, but he forced it smaller. Slower. Every breath was an act of balance now. Too deep, and the rubble pressed down. Too shallow, and he’d choke on the dust still clinging to his throat. He was awake now. Fully. No more haze. No more drifting thoughts. Just the weight. The dust. The sound of his own pulse in his ears. If he moved too much, the whole pile would remember what it was capable of. Every breath shifted the stones by fractions. Every shift tempted gravity to finish the job. The Eyrie hadn’t just collapsed. It had buried him. And all he could do — the only thing — was stay very, very still... ...and hope the next person to find him wasn’t the seven-foot steroid golem that put him here in the first place. Ch 2 – Liminal David didn’t know if he’d blacked out again, or if time had just slithered sideways without telling him. There was no sky to track. No light to shift. Just the weight, the ache, and the slow, dry scrape of dust collecting in his lungs with every shallow breath. Random pains seemed to shift or bloom when he hadn’t been paying attention. His right arm was still a blank in his perception. Maybe asleep. Maybe broken. Hard to say. Harder to care. It wasn’t coming back online anytime soon either way. His left was another story. That one still worked, still braced above him, still bearing the load. His forearm wedged between his face and the nearest stone, keeping it from finishing the job. The muscles in his shoulder screamed now — not in bursts, but in a steady, smoldering burn, like fire left to smother under its own ash. A pain too quiet to scream, too loud to ignore. He hadn’t dared move it. Not for... minutes? Hours? He had taken to resting its weight against his forehead, but the pressure of the stones above still kept the muscle tight. However long it had been, the limb was shaking now. Not much. Just the tiniest tremble. But in a place like this, tiny had teeth. At some point, he started hearing things. A voice? Maybe. Probably not. Prolonged silence did weird things to a person’s mind, and with this headache, it was likely just his own thoughts bouncing off him. No, that wasn’t it... it was more of a yell. Far off. Muffled. Familiar in a way that made his chest seize up for reasons he couldn’t quite name. Was that him, or something real? He held his breath, forcing himself to listen through the roar of his own pulse. There. Something again. Footsteps? The crunch of sand under boots? Soft voices filtered in through the silence — so faint he almost missed them. “Why is he chasing her like that?” “Because it’s Jill. Nemesis sees that uniform and gets tunnel vision. I’d be shocked if he wasn’t chasing her.” “So, then we... what? Just let her get chased?” “Well yeah. She’ll be ok. We can get things done in the meantime.” David blinked slowly, grit dragging across his lashes. He hadn’t imagined it. Someone was out there. Outside the Eyrie. Getting closer . It was surreal. Voices drifting past like it was just another day in the Fog, laughing about killer patterns and survivor bait while he lay crushed in the dark, half-buried under a structure that wanted to finish folding him like a lawn chair. His sanity creaked under the weight of it. A small prickle of panic clawed at the back of his throat. He couldn’t tell where the voices were coming from just from the sound alone — whether they were near the Eyrie or just passing by . He couldn’t wave. Couldn’t even shift enough to make noise without risking a full cave-in. But if they didn’t come into the building... if they didn’t see the rubble... They’d miss him entirely. He didn’t have the luxury of waiting. He had to try. He swallowed. The grit in his throat made the motion grind. He tried to shout. Nothing. A wheeze. A cough. Pain flared in his ribs as a stone shifted threateningly and jabbed his side. “Here,” he rasped, a thread of voice scraping out like broken glass. “Hey—!” It wasn’t much. Just two syllables and a thread of panic. But they scratched their way through the cracks. And Dwight stopped walking. Mid-step. Boot still half-hovering over the sand. “...Wait.” Felix paused beside him, glancing back. “What is it?” “I — hold on.” Dwight tilted his head, gaze flicking toward the building. “I thought I heard something.” Felix didn’t catch it, whatever it was. But Dwight had that look — the one he got right before finding a teammate bleeding out behind a wall no one else thought to check. Felix had been in enough trials by now to know better than to ignore the man’s instincts. He followed him toward the Eyrie’s doors. Inside, the Eyrie was eerily still. Books. Way too much sand. A lone generator, cold and ignored. And a pile of rubble where half of a staircase used to be. “Looks like the walkway above collapsed,” Felix murmured, eyes tracing the damage. “Took part of the stairwell with it. I wasn’t even aware the landscape could collapse like that in a trial.” “Things have been weird lately. Who knows what’s possible anymore.” The Eyrie had always been a weird mix of hideous planning and impressive masonry. Still, this was new. He caught himself studying the fault lines, noting where the arch had folded under its own weight — a perfect storm of tension and force — when Dwight’s voice cut through his thoughts, reminding him why they were there. “Hello?” A sound broke the quiet. Small. Choked. Like someone trying to stifle a cough. Felix froze mid-step, spine straightening instinctively. “Okay. That I heard.” Dwight was already turning toward the rubble, expression sharpening. It was an odd place to hunker down. Too exposed, no clear escape route. Although, if Jill was outside running Nemesis in circles, and he and Felix were right there... “David?” he called out, tone tight. “’m here,” came the thin reply — warped by grit and pressure, but unmistakably human. “Could use a hand, tho.” Felix’s head snapped toward the rubble, alarm flickering beneath his usual calm. “Did that just come from inside the collapse?” “Wait—shit,” Dwight surged forward without waiting for confirmation, boots kicking up sand. “Are you okay?! What happened?” No reply at first. Just the dull sound of stone shifting as David let his head rest against his arm again — too drained to move, too relieved not to. His body shook once, tension flaring and failing all at once. “Just get me out of here,” he muttered. “ Carefully . This shit is held together by spite.” Dwight and Felix traded a glance — silent, serious — before dropping to assess the pile. “We’ve got you,” Dwight said, already brushing grit away with careful hands and moving to grip at the stones. “Just stay with us.” David barely exhaled. A thread of breath. A flicker of disbelief. Help had come. Now all they had to do... was not kill him with it. Chapter 3 – Breakpoint The digging inevitably slowed after a time. Not because they were tiring — but because the pile was starting to respond. Felix had been directing the work with surgical precision, calling out load-bearing stones and picking targets with care, but even then... progress was agonizingly slow. Dwight’s idle chatter had kept David distracted for a while, the relief of not being alone having given him something else to focus on, but it did little to disguise the feeling of weight shifting as they worked. Every piece of rubble shifted something. Each stone removed sent new tremors through the makeshift tomb, and David felt it everywhere. The weight on his chest didn’t ease. If anything, it pressed in harder, like the structure above was getting impatient. Every time he exhaled, the space around his ribs compressed a little more. Tiny, incremental shifts. No sudden movements. Just the slow, inevitable collapse of geometry. Felix called something from above — an update, maybe. Dwight's voice replied, closer now, strained and anxious. David couldn’t make out the words. All he could hear was stone — the subtle grind of weight against weight. The whisper of pressure shifting in search of somewhere else to land. His right shoulder had started to burn. The numb, heavy blankness of his pinned arm was waking up again — coming back to him in flashes of static pain. Each inhale was a losing battle. Each exhale left him less to work with. The air that left his lungs didn’t come back — not fully. The space around him shrank by fractions, inch by inch, until it felt like the rubble was learning to breathe with him. Like a snake coiling tighter with every motion, the stones above stole space his body couldn’t reclaim. The panic didn’t crash down all at once. It seeped in quiet at the edges, crawling like cold fingers along the base of his skull. He pushed it back as best he could every time it flared up, but it kept coming back. He could feel the pile sliding. Not the big rocks. Not yet. Just the little ones. Pebbles crawling over his arm. Grit dusting down into the hollows of his collarbone. Something sharp shifted under his ribs — he couldn’t tell if it was a rock or a cracked bone. The dust thickened, burning his eyes, clawing its way down his throat. He coughed again, this one violent enough to spike fresh pain through his chest. Still, he stayed quiet. The words wanted out. He locked them behind his teeth. “...getting close,” Dwight cut through from above. “I think I see his shoulder — yeah, that’s fabric. That’s him.” “Careful,” Felix warned. “Don’t pull — just clear around it.” David tried to nod. Couldn’t. The pressure was too tight. “You’re doing fine. Just... don’t stop.” There was a tremble in his voice he couldn’t quite hide. “David?” Dwight’s voice lowered. “You okay?” He grunted. “Still here.” Technically true. It didn’t matter that he couldn’t draw a full breath anymore. Didn’t matter that every muscle left was burning just trying to hold his arm up between his skull and the stone. If he told them it was getting worse, they’d panic. If they panicked, they’d rush. If they rushed, they’d make a mistake. “I’m fine. Just shut up and dig.” Each exhale cost him ground he couldn’t take back. Chest sinking shallower. Lungs compressing further with every ragged breath. The edges of his vision sparked, dust and shadows closing in like a tunnel he couldn’t claw out of. A narrow small gap opened as a stone was pulled away. Just large enough for Dwight to push his arm through. David flinched as fingers found his, wrapping around the hand still braced against the weight. “You’re doing good,” Dwight said gently, voice tight but even. “Just keep talking to me. We’ve got you. You’re gonna be okay.” David clenched his jaw, willing himself not to panic. He focused on the contact. Not the dust. Not the stone. Not the crush of air that wouldn’t come back in. It wasn’t much. But it was the closest to outside he’d been in over an hour. “You better be right,” he rasped. “Don’t suppose you found a crowbar down here with me?” That got a light chuckle from Dwight, the soft sound easing back some of the anxiety. This was good. They had opened up some space. Let in some light. Just that much closer to getting back into the open air again. He could handle this. It was hardly the worst trial he had gone through, anyways. “Alright,” Felix called. “Top layer’s mostly clear on this side. I can see the shape of him — his shoulder’s wedged under that flat slab. If we shift it straight up and back—” CRACK. It wasn’t a collapse. Just a single, fist-sized chunk of sandstone coming loose from somewhere higher up. But it landed square on the pile, driving a lower stone into David’s hip like a hammer. He jerked — instinctive, immediate — and the pile answered . The weight on his chest dropped half an inch, his body compressing under it like a sponge. Dust billowed into his mouth. The stone above his head scraped down hard against his forearm, and the muscles screamed — finally reaching their limit after holding for far too long. And somewhere deep inside... something snapped . He gasped — a full breath for the first time in minutes — and the sudden expansion made everything shift again. He shoved hard against the nearest stone, pressing his shoulder against it, kicking down to try and twist his hip away from the pressure. It wasn’t a choice, but pure reflex. He couldn’t help it. His body demanded oxygen. Demanded motion. Demanded freedom . “David — stop ! You’re making it worse!” Felix’s voice cracked as stone shifted overhead. But David wasn’t listening. He was gone. Every muscle seized in panic, heaving against the crush, desperate to escape. His thoughts blurred into static, a single command screaming louder than pain, louder than logic: OUT . His left arm tore free of its space, elbow crashing the side of the pile as he tried to lever his torso upward — sheer instinct, blind and useless. The stone he’d been holding off finally dropped, slamming down against his forehead with a brutal scrape, narrowly missing his eye. The shift collapsed the fragile gap Dwight had carved out. The moment he felt the rush of air vanish, Dwight yanked his arm back with a sharp yell, stone rasping down his forearm and tearing a line through both skin and jacket in a single clean snag. He stumbled back hard, clutching his wrist. “He’s panicking!” “David, stop ! You have to calm down!” Felix snapped, already scrambling to find a grip on the nearest rock. “You’re going to bring it all down!” David was beyond listening, the insistent cries of his teammates drowned out by the screaming in his own mind. He thrashed — not in any useful direction, not toward rescue — just against everything . His limbs struck out at pressure points, searching for a weakness in the crush, but found only more stone. He wasn’t fighting them. He was fighting everything . The dust clawing down his throat. The weight grinding in around his ribs. The dark. The silence. The sheer wrongness of his body being unable to move, to breathe, to be . Cause and effect had left the building. Reason was gone. There was only movement now — fast, feral, unthinking. A primal spasm that flung his hips sideways, body twisting toward a space that didn’t exist, trying to be elsewhere by sheer force alone. Above him, Felix barely caught a loose chunk before it tumbled. He flung it away, hand already grabbing at another. “He’s going to destabilize everything,” he snapped. “Help me get this clear!” Dwight scrambled back to the pile, skidding on grit, blood streaking down his arm. “David, please—!” For a moment, it looked like he might actually get free. David’s shoulder shoved upward, scraping stone aside with a jagged screech. One slab near his head slipped loose, dragging a pale gouge in the rock as it rolled — and a gap opened. Light. Air. But then gravity remembered him again. The rubble poured down, sweeping across the pile from the remains of the staircase above. A chunk near the top shifted, dislodging the stone above his left arm. It dropped — hard — pinning him sideways and dragging his arm down with it. Grit sprayed out in all directions as the weight surged. The weight dropped, slow but unrelenting, filling every open space. The weight crushed inward, and David’s chest folded beneath it. His ribs compressed, oxygen stolen before he could even try to reclaim it. His vision exploded into white — too tight, too loud, too much — and the world tipped sideways into silence. “Felix, the center’s falling!” Dwight shouted. “I see it — brace that corner — shit — David! ” Another stone went flying as Dwight tore at the edge of the collapse. Dust plumed up, stinging his eyes. “David?! David, are you okay?” Felix stepped hesitantly back from the rubble. He was scanning — eyes darting over the pile, cataloguing what had shifted, what progress had all been lost. “Did you see where he moved? Is he—?” “I... I don’t know.” Dwight’s voice cracked. “The gap’s gone. I can’t tell if he shifted or—” The words died in the stillness. No voice answered. Just the hush of settling dust... and the soft, steady grind of stone. Ch 4 – Extraction Dwight dove back into the rubble, tearing at loose stones with shaking hands. He tried for one of the heavier chunks, but his injured arm screamed in protest, the sharp throb in his wrist making it hard to lift, and the blood running down his palm left his grip weak and clumsy. He was aiming for the same gap he’d carved out earlier — hoping, praying it hadn’t fully collapsed. But the pile had shifted too far. Every reference point was gone. He was digging blind. It wasn’t until his third failed lift that he realized he was alone. He glanced up, confused — and saw Felix a few feet back, standing stiffly in the dust. His eyes were locked on the rubble, unfocused and distant, his posture rigid. One hand still held a small chunk of sandstone he hadn’t dropped. His fingers twitched around it absently, but the rest of him didn’t move. His chest rose and fell in quick, shallow bursts. Breathing too fast. Not blinking. Felix wasn’t frozen. He was folding . Quietly crumpling in on himself as the panic overtook him. “Felix!” Dwight’s voice cracked as he shouted across the rubble. “ Come on — get over here! ” No reply. Swearing under his breath, Dwight scrambled over, grabbing for Felix’s arm — only to find it stiff, locked in place like it didn’t belong to him. Up close, he could hear it: a soft murmur under Felix’s breath, looping fragments of thought, barely audible over the rasp of his shallow breathing. “It shouldn’t have collapsed... I made the call... I should have seen it—” His eyes weren’t tracking. He wasn’t blinking. Just staring through the pile like it was a grave he’d dug himself. Dwight’s stomach sank. Felix wasn’t just panicking. He was gone . Disassociating hard — caught in the guilt spiral, stuck in the feedback loop. If someone didn’t break him out of it fast, he was going to shut down completely. Panic flared — not at the rocks, but at Felix . At the distant stare, the static loop of words, the sinking posture. He’d seen it before. Survivors slipping inward. Folding in on themselves mid-trial, locked so deep inside they couldn’t hear their name shouted right beside them. Between the mental spirals and whatever the Fog did to people to prolong pain, some of them didn’t resurface for days. With Jill outside keeping Nemesis busy, if he didn’t do something fast, he was about to lose his only help. Something sparked in the back of his mind. Something he had seen other survivors do in moments like this. It didn’t always work, but... Before he could think about it too much and potentially talk himself out of it, he did the only thing he’d ever seen bring someone else around in a hurry. He slapped him. Hard. The sound cracked through the rubble louder than it should’ve — knuckles against cheekbone, clean and sharp. Felix hit the ground with a startled grunt, blinking up at Dwight in confused alarm. “Oh my god—oh my god I’m so sorry —I didn’t mean to—shit—I just— you weren’t there , I didn’t know what to do—are you okay??” Felix blinked again. Raised a hand to his cheek. “...Did you just hit me?” “I panicked!” Dwight squeaked. Felix stared at him for a second longer — then huffed a breath, somewhere between a laugh and a scoff. Dwight crouched down, offering a hand. “I didn’t mean to hit you that hard, I just... I needed help.” Felix took it, still half-stunned. “Help? Right, we were — shit , sorry... yeah, I’m ok.” The moment settled between them like dust, reorienting Felix back onto the pile as focus swept away whatever thoughts had tried to take him. If Dwight could break out of it, so could he. There was no time to dwell. The pile had shifted too much — David’s position could’ve been anywhere by now. What was once a half-buried incline off the staircase wall had slumped into something closer to a landslide: jagged, lopsided, and barely holding its shape. Each motion sent fine debris cascading across the surface like snow. Felix and Dwight dove back in, tearing away anything unstable — grabbing whatever stones looked like they’d cause trouble and chucking them down the slope. Dwight was working from memory, fingers bleeding from grit and broken edges, trying to trace the last place he’d touched David’s hand. The gap he’d made was gone. Swallowed up in the collapse. At least only the upper layers seemed to still be unstable, though. As he worked his way down, the larger stones seemed to have settled into something less chaotic, and could be worked around easily enough. It didn’t take long for him to have tunneled partway into the pile itself, managing to get nearly half his torso in, pilling smaller debris out and firing it behind him. David had been moving around a lot, but there was no way he had gotten that far from where he had been. If Dwight could re-open the area where he had last seen him, chances were good that he could find him again. Digging his fingers in around a good-sized chunk and wiggling it free, he finally spotted a flash of red fabric “I got him!” Dwight shouted. “I—I think I got him!” He cleared a ragged channel around the shape of an arm — elbow half-bent, the length vanishing under the bulk of jacket. He followed it upward, hand dragging through loose gravel and crumbled plaster, until his fingers brushed against something solid. Forehead. Cold and tacky with blood. “Felix — here! I’ve got his head!” Felix scrambled over, slipping on the
